extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy (lecture attendees, philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: A series of early-20th-century lectures (William James) presenting pragmatism as a method and theory of truth and offering normative criteria for evaluating philosophical theories — emphasis on verifiability, practical consequences, temperament, and mediation between empiricism and religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament influences philosophizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperament is a factor in all philosophizing; a philosopher's temperament 'loads the evidence' for him and gives him a stronger bias than strictly objective premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that personal temperament (tender-minded or tough-minded) shapes what kinds of arguments and conclusions a philosopher favors; recommends admitting this premise for clarity in philosophical discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tender-minded vs. tough-minded typology
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasting types of philosophical temper: THE TENDER-MINDED (Rationalistic, Intellectualistic, Idealistic, Optimistic, Religious, Free-willist, Monistic, Dogmatical) and THE TOUGH-MINDED (Empiricist, Sensationalistic, Materialistic, Pessimistic, Irreligious, Fatalistic, Pluralistic, Sceptical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these trait-lists to classify, understand, and critique philosophical positions; recognizes many people are mixtures rather than pure types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must connect with concrete human life
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory philosophy should 'make some positive connexion with this actual world of finite human lives' rather than remain remote and vacuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely abstract systems that have no bearing on concrete facts, joys, sorrows, or practical human concerns; seek philosophies that inform lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine scientific loyalty to facts with human values
rubrics_metrics.description: The desired philosophy 'will combine both things, the scientific loyalty to facts and willingness to take account of them... but also the old confidence in human values and the resultant spontaneity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a mediating stance that preserves intimacy with empirical facts while maintaining moral/religious/human ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unreality and sterile abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of rationalistic systems as unreal: such systems are 'simple, clean and noble' refuges from the messy world; they 'breathe out nothing but refinement' and are inadequate for the fact-loving mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of philosophical constructions that are elegant but disconnected from the actual phenomena they purport to explain (examples: Leibnitz's theodicy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatism as mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism can 'remain religious like the rationalisms, but at the same time, like the empiricisms, it can preserve the richest intimacy with facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical systems by their capacity to reconcile opposing demands (e.g., facts vs. religion), acting as a middle path rather than an extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability as criterion of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement with reality 'means verifiability.' Verifiability is defined as the 'ability to guide us prosperously through experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge claims by their practical, experiential testability and their capacity to guide successful action; completed formal proof may not always be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as practical good (truth-as-use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true is 'the good in the way of belief'; 'Truth is a good, like health, wealth, etc.' Truth is expedient thinking and grows over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess propositions by the practical benefits of believing them (their consequences), and by how their acceptance aids human purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: New beliefs must account for older truths
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming new beliefs, 'Older truth always has to be kept account of' — new beliefs must take the body of previously established truths into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing revisions or new doctrines, show how they accommodate and explain the successes of prior beliefs rather than gratuitously discarding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate alternatives by what they 'promise'
rubrics_metrics.description: In metaphysical disputes 'the pragmatic issue at stake... is what do the alternatives PROMISE.' The appeal of a theory lies in the practical outcomes and possibilities it suggests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare theories by the concrete promises they entail (what possibilities, powers, or unifications they open up) rather than by abstract a priori elegance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose monistic dogmatism; follow empirical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: We 'must oppose monistic dogmatism and follow empirical findings.' Monistic absolutism should not override empirical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor pluralism or empirically informed positions when monistic doctrines conflict with observed facts; keep doctrines revisable in light of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the evolutionary/developmental character of common sense and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Common-sense concepts (space, time, things, kinds, cause, law) came gradually into use; knowledge grows and earlier ways remain as stages in mental evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conceptual frameworks as historically and psychologically evolved; when evaluating theories, consider their relation to common-sense stages and scientific/philosophical developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatism 'unstiffens' discussion and reduces quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism 'unstiffens discussion' by focusing on practical consequences and by mediating between opposed temperaments and doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pragmatic criteria to deflate purely verbal or metaphysical disputes by translating them into questions about practical effects and experiential differences.
